title: Week 2 assignment: Comparing postoperative pain-management protocols
text:
Study description
A clinical research team compares a standard postoperative pain-management protocol with an enhanced protocol for patients undergoing elective knee replacement surgery. The team wants to estimate the average effect of the enhanced protocol across hospitals and understand how much its effect varies between hospitals.
The study includes 12 hospitals representing a wider population of hospitals treating similar patients. Within each hospital, 30 patients are randomly assigned to the two protocols: 15 receive standard care and 15 receive the enhanced protocol. Each patient receives one protocol and contributes one pain measurement 24 hours after surgery, giving 360 observations.
Pain is measured using a visual analogue scale, recorded from 0 to 10, where 0 represents no pain and 10 represents the worst imaginable pain. Scores are recorded to one decimal place. Lower scores indicate less pain. These are simulated teaching data.


Dataset
Each row represents one patient.



Variable
Description




patient_id
Unique identifier for the patient


hospital
Hospital, labelled Hospital 01 to Hospital 12


protocol
Pain-management protocol: Standard or Enhanced


pain_score
Pain score 24 hours after surgery, on the 0–10 scale



Express protocol differences as enhanced minus standard, in pain-score points. A negative difference indicates lower pain under the enhanced protocol.


Analysis tasks

Describe the design. Identify the experimental unit and grouping variable, and explain how the protocols were assigned within hospitals. Describe the population to which the research team aims to generalize.
Explore the data. Calculate the number of patients, mean pain score, and standard deviation for each protocol within each hospital. Create an interaction plot with hospitals on the horizontal axis and one line per protocol connecting the observed means. Discuss the patterns in standard-care pain levels and protocol differences across hospitals.
Fit a random-intercept and treatment-slope model. Include protocol as a fixed effect and a correlated random intercept and protocol slope for hospital.
Report and interpret the results. Report and interpret the fixed and random effects to answer the research team’s questions about the average protocol effect and variation between hospitals. Support your conclusions with appropriate statistical evidence.
Check the model and conclude. Examine the conditional-residual-versus-fitted plot and the Normal Q-Q plot, and comment on the model assumptions. Write a short conclusion answering the research team’s question. Include the average protocol difference, its uncertainty, appropriate units, and what the analysis suggests about variation in effects across hospitals.

Explain your findings in the context of postoperative pain management and include units where appropriate.


Report and submission
Submit a report created using Quarto that presents your analysis, results, and interpretations, using the template provided in the Downloads section below.
The template follows the Week 1 report format. It includes a setup chunk that uses pak to install the required packages if needed and then loads them. Follow the installation instructions in Lab 1 to prepare pak. The setup chunk runs during rendering and stays hidden in the report.
Submit both the completed Quarto source file (.qmd) and the rendered HTML report. Keep your analysis code, results, and figures visible, and accompany them with your interpretations.






NoteHelp with Quarto





Save the report template in your week2 folder and the dataset in week2/data. Read the dataset using read.csv("data/postoperative_pain.csv").
Open the template in RStudio. Replace Your name with your name and replace the italic prompts with your own writing. Add your analysis code to the labelled chunks. To run code as you work, use the Run button in a chunk or select lines and press Ctrl+Enter on Windows/Linux or Cmd+Enter on macOS.
To produce the complete HTML report, save the file and press Render. Alternatively, with week2 as the current directory in the RStudio Terminal, run:
quarto render report_template.qmd
If you rename the template, use your chosen filename in this command. Rendering executes your code in a fresh R session, so include the data import and all analysis steps in the document.
Keep eval: true and echo: true in the YAML header so your analysis runs and its code and results appear in the report. The setup chunk uses include: false to install and load packages while keeping that preparation hidden. Leave warnings visible while developing the analysis so you can investigate any fitting issues.
See Help with Quarto in the Week 1 assignment for more detail about document structure and execution settings.

title: Beyond MLR Lab 4: Random intercepts and treatment slopes
text:
In Lab 3, five laboratories compared a standard treatment with an experimental treatment. Each laboratory randomly assigned 10 independent cell-culture plates to each treatment. The outcome was the percentage of the original wound area that had closed after 48 hours. Each plate was measured once, giving 100 observations. These are simulated teaching data.
The interaction plot below recalls the observed treatment means from Lab 3. Each line represents one treatment, and the vertical gap between the lines is the observed treatment difference in a laboratory.



Observed mean wound closure in each laboratory, reproduced from Lab 3.


We now regard these laboratories as representing a wider population of laboratories using the same experimental protocol. Our question is: What is the average treatment effect across that population, and how much do treatment effects vary between laboratories? Generalizing in this way relies on the laboratories being relevant to the population of interest.
By the end of this lab, you should be able to fit a random-intercept and treatment-slope model, interpret its variance components and intercept-slope correlation, interpret the population-average treatment effect and its uncertainty, and assess the conditional residuals.






NoteWorking through the lab



Run the code in order in an R script and record your answers to the questions. As in the earlier labs, the page supplies analysis code and you generate the results yourself. The plot above is provided as background from Lab 3.

title: Beyond MLR Lab 4: Random intercepts and treatment slopes
section: Allow both the intercept and treatment effect to vary
text:
Allow both the intercept and treatment effect to vary
Let \(Y_{ij}\) be the closure for plate \(i\) in laboratory \(j\), with \(T_{ij}=0\) for standard treatment and \(T_{ij}=1\) for experimental treatment. We specify
\[
Y_{ij}=\beta_0+c_j+(\beta_1+d_j)T_{ij}+\varepsilon_{ij}.
\]

\(\beta_0\) is the standard-treatment mean averaged over the population of laboratories.
\(\beta_1\) is the experimental-minus-standard effect averaged over that population.
\(c_j\) is laboratory \(j\)’s deviation from the population standard-treatment mean.
\(d_j\) is laboratory \(j\)’s deviation from the population-average treatment effect.
\(\varepsilon_{ij}\) is the remaining individual plate error.

Thus, laboratory \(j\) has intercept \(\beta_0+c_j\) and treatment effect \(\beta_1+d_j\). The treatment effect is called a slope because it describes the change in expected closure when treatment changes from 0 (standard) to 1 (experimental).
The laboratory deviations follow a joint Normal distribution:
\[
\begin{pmatrix}c_j\\d_j\end{pmatrix}
\sim N\!\left[
\begin{pmatrix}0\\0\end{pmatrix},
\begin{pmatrix}\sigma_c^2&\sigma_{cd}\\\sigma_{cd}&\sigma_d^2\end{pmatrix}
\right].
\]
The diagonal entries describe variation in standard-treatment means and in treatment effects. The off-diagonal entry, \(\sigma_{cd}\), is their covariance. We allow the two deviations within a laboratory to be correlated. Deviation pairs are independent across laboratories.
Individual errors are independent Normal variables with a common variance,
\[
\varepsilon_{ij}\overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}N(0,\sigma^2),
\]
and are independent of the laboratory deviations.






ImportantQuestion 1



What do a positive \(c_j\) and a positive \(d_j\) mean in this experiment? What is the expected closure under each treatment in laboratory \(j\)? Identify the term that allows treatment effects to vary between laboratories.

title: Beyond MLR Lab 4: Random intercepts and treatment slopes
section: Fit the random-intercept and slope model
text:
Fit the random-intercept and slope model

model_random <- lmer(
  closure ~ treatment + (1 + treatment | laboratory),
  data = wound,
  REML = TRUE
)
summary(model_random)

The formula has two parts:

closure ~ treatment specifies the population-average intercept and treatment effect.
(1 + treatment | laboratory) adds a laboratory-specific random intercept and random treatment slope, allowing them to be correlated.

Laboratory is the grouping variable. We use restricted maximum likelihood (REML) to estimate the variance components, as in Lab 2.
The summary separates the fixed effects, which describe the population averages, from the random effects, which describe variation around those averages. In the fixed-effect table, (Intercept) estimates \(\beta_0\) and treatmentExperimental estimates \(\beta_1\).






NoteThe intercept is included by default



The 1 denotes an intercept and is included by default: (treatment | laboratory) is equivalent to (1 + treatment | laboratory). Both specify a random intercept and treatment slope, allowing them to be correlated. We write 1 + treatment here to make both components visible. Similarly, the fixed-effects formula closure ~ treatment already includes an intercept.








ImportantQuestion 2



Identify and interpret the estimated population-average standard-treatment mean and the estimated population-average treatment effect. How is the treatment effect in a particular laboratory represented in the model?

title: Beyond MLR Lab 4: Random intercepts and treatment slopes
text:
Display the variance components
Use VarCorr() to display the estimated variance components and intercept-slope correlation. Setting comp = "Variance" displays the variances; the default displays standard deviations.

print(VarCorr(model_random), comp = "Variance")

The three variances have units of squared percentage points with treatment coded 0/1. The Corr column gives the intercept-slope correlation.







Component
Interpretation




Intercept variance, \(\sigma_c^2\)
Variation in standard-treatment means between laboratories


Treatment-slope variance, \(\sigma_d^2\)
Variation in treatment effects between laboratories


Residual variance, \(\sigma^2\)
Variation among individual plates around their laboratory-specific treatment mean

title: Beyond MLR Lab 4: Random intercepts and treatment slopes
text:
Interpret the intercept-slope correlation
The intercept-slope covariance describes how laboratory deviations in standard-treatment means and treatment effects vary together. The correlation expresses this relationship on a standardized scale by dividing the covariance by the product of the two standard deviations:
\[
\widehat{\rho}_{cd}
=\frac{\widehat{\sigma}_{cd}}
{\sqrt{\widehat{\sigma}_c^2\widehat{\sigma}_d^2}}.
\]
R provides this estimated correlation in the Corr column of the VarCorr() output above.
The intercept-slope correlation describes the relationship between laboratory deviations in standard-treatment means and treatment effects. A positive correlation means that laboratories with higher standard-treatment means tend to have larger treatment effects. A negative correlation means that they tend to have smaller treatment effects.






ImportantQuestion 3



Identify the estimated intercept variance, treatment-slope variance and residual variance. Which source has the largest estimated variance? Identify the estimated intercept-slope correlation in the output and interpret its sign in the wound-healing setting.

title: Beyond MLR Lab 2: Modeling center as a random effect
text:
In Lab 1, we analyzed a simulated rehabilitation trial involving 120 patients after knee replacement in six centers. Each center assigned 10 patients to standard care and 10 to enhanced rehabilitation. We fitted a model containing separate fixed center effects.
We now keep the same randomized block design and the same question: What is the difference in expected six-minute walk distance at 12 weeks between enhanced and standard care, and how precisely is it estimated? Instead of estimating separate fixed center parameters, we describe center contributions using a distribution. This also allows us to quantify variation between centers.
By the end of this lab, you should be able to fit a random-intercept model, interpret its treatment estimate and uncertainty, interpret its variance components and intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC), and assess its conditional residuals.

title: Beyond MLR Lab 2: Modeling center as a random effect
text:
Extract the variances
VarCorr() returns the estimated variance components. Converting its output to a data frame makes it straightforward to use the values in a calculation.

variance_components <- as.data.frame(VarCorr(model_random))
variance_components

center_variance <- variance_components$vcov[
  variance_components$grp == "center"
]
patient_variance <- variance_components$vcov[
  variance_components$grp == "Residual"
]

c(center_variance = center_variance,
  patient_variance = patient_variance)

The vcov column contains variances; the sdcor column contains their standard deviations for this model. Use the variances in the intraclass correlation coefficient calculation.

title: Beyond MLR Lab 2: Modeling center as a random effect
text:
Introduce the intraclass correlation
After accounting for treatment, the remaining outcome variation consists of the shared center contribution and the individual error:
\[
u_{ij}=c_j+\varepsilon_{ij},
\qquad \operatorname{Var}(u_{ij})=\sigma_c^2+\sigma^2.
\]
For two different patients in the same center, the shared center contribution gives
\[
\operatorname{Cov}(u_{ij},u_{kj})=\sigma_c^2 \quad (i\ne k).
\]
Dividing this covariance by the common variance gives the intraclass correlation coefficient:
\[
\mathrm{ICC}=\frac{\sigma_c^2}{\sigma_c^2+\sigma^2}.
\]
This has two connected interpretations:

The proportion of outcome variance remaining after accounting for treatment that is attributable to differences between centers.
The correlation between outcomes of two different patients in the same center, after accounting for their treatments and averaging over the modeled center distribution.

If we condition on a particular center effect as well as treatment, only the independent individual errors remain. The within-center correlation above arises because patients share a random center contribution.

icc <- center_variance / (center_variance + patient_variance)
icc







ImportantQuestion 4



Calculate the intraclass correlation coefficient. Interpret it both as a variance proportion and as a within-center correlation. What correlation does the model assume for patients in different centers, after accounting for treatment?








TipModel answer 4



Using the estimated variances,
\[
\widehat{\mathrm{ICC}}
= \frac{513.81}{513.81 + 564.76}
\approx 0.476.
\]
About 47.64% of the outcome variance remaining after accounting for treatment is attributable to differences between centers. The remaining 52.36% is individual variation within centers.
For two different patients in the same center, the estimated correlation after accounting for treatment is about 0.48, averaging over the modeled center distribution. They share the same random center contribution. For patients in different centers, the model assumes a correlation of zero because their center contributions and individual errors are independent.

title: Beyond MLR Lab 1: Modeling center as a fixed effect
text:
We return to the rehabilitation trial from the lecture. In this simulated study, 120 patients recovering from knee replacement receive either standard care or an enhanced rehabilitation program. Standard care consists of weekly physiotherapy and home exercises; enhanced care adds a weekly supervised session. The outcome is the distance walked during a six-minute walk test at 12 weeks, measured in meters. A larger distance indicates better walking performance.
The study includes six centers. Within each center, 10 patients are randomly assigned to standard care and 10 to enhanced care. This is a randomized block design, with center as the blocking factor. These are simulated teaching data.
Our question is: What is the estimated difference in expected walking distance between enhanced and standard care, and how precisely is it estimated? We will explore differences between centers and fit a model that includes center as a fixed effect.
By the end of this lab, you should be able to visualize treatment and center differences, fit and interpret the fixed-effects model, quantify uncertainty about the treatment effect, and check the model assumptions.






NoteWorking through the lab



Run the code in order in an R script, and record your answers to the questions. The lab page shows the code; you generate the results yourself.

Install pak once
An R package provides additional functions, for example for drawing figures or fitting statistical models. Throughout this course, we will use the package manager pak to install the packages we need. It also handles their dependencies: other packages they need to work.

Use pak throughout the course
Installing a package saves it on your computer. Loading a package makes its functions available in the current R session. Installed packages remain available between sessions, but you need to load them again when you start a new session.
We will follow the same pattern in each lab: load pak with library(pak), use pkg_install() to install the packages needed for that lab, and then load those packages with library(). The pak package manager checks the required packages and their dependencies and keeps already installed versions when they meet the requirements.
For this lab, we need ggplot2 for figures and dplyr for summaries. Add the following code to the beginning of your script and run it. If pak asks whether to proceed, confirm the installation and wait for it to finish.

pkg_install(c("ggplot2", "dplyr"))

Now load the packages for your analysis. Keep these commands in your script so that they run each time you start the lab in a new R session.

title: Beyond MLR Lab 1: Modeling center as a fixed effect
text:
Read the data
With week1 as your working directory and the dataset saved in its data subfolder, run the following code. If R cannot find the file, check getwd(), the folder containing the CSV file, and its filename.

rehab <- read.csv("data/rehabilitation_week1.csv")

# Specify the order of the categories explicitly.
rehab$treatment <- factor(rehab$treatment,
                          levels = c("Standard", "Enhanced"))
rehab$center <- factor(rehab$center,
                       levels = paste("Center", LETTERS[1:6]))

head(rehab)
str(rehab)
table(rehab$center, rehab$treatment)

Each row represents one patient. The variables are center, treatment, and distance (six-minute walk distance in meters). A factor tells R that a variable represents categories. The order of the factor levels will matter when we choose how to represent these categories in the model.






ImportantQuestion 1



Check the allocation table. How many patients are in each treatment group within each center? Why is this allocation useful when comparing the treatments?

There are 10 patients per treatment in each center, so each center contributes 20 patients, each treatment has 60 patients, and there are 120 patients in total.
Randomization within centers allows the two treatments to be compared among patients from the same center. Equal allocation gives both treatments the same mix of centers, balancing the contribution of center differences to the overall treatment comparison. Accounting for center can improve precision by removing between-center differences from the residual variation.

title: Beyond MLR Lab 1: Modeling center as a fixed effect
text:
Specify the model
Let \(Y_{ij}\) be the outcome for patient \(i\) in center \(j\), and let \(T_{ij}\) indicate the patient’s treatment. We include an intercept \(\beta_0\), a treatment coefficient \(\beta_1\), and a fixed contribution \(c_j\) for each center:
\[
Y_{ij} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 T_{ij} + c_j + \varepsilon_{ij},
\qquad \varepsilon_{ij} \overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim} N(0,\sigma^2).
\]
Without a constraint, increasing the intercept and decreasing every center contribution by the same amount would leave the model’s predictions unchanged. To define these parameters uniquely, we require the six center contributions to sum to zero:
\[
c_A+c_B+c_C+c_D+c_E+c_F=0.
\]
The model assumes that the expected treatment difference is the same in every center. After accounting for treatment and center, the remaining errors are assumed to be independent and identically distributed Normal variables with mean zero and common variance.
To fit this model in R, we explicitly set how each factor is represented numerically. We use dummy coding for treatment to define \(T_{ij}\) and effects coding for center so that R estimates the center deviations specified above.

title: Beyond MLR Lab 1: Modeling center as a fixed effect
text:
Code treatment using dummy coding
With dummy coding, one category is the reference. We use standard care as the reference and represent treatment by a single indicator:



Treatment
Indicator \(T_{ij}\)




Standard
0


Enhanced
1



Within center \(j\), the expected standard-care outcome is \(\beta_0+c_j\), and the expected enhanced-care outcome is \(\beta_0+\beta_1+c_j\). The treatment coefficient \(\beta_1\) is therefore the enhanced-minus-standard difference.

# The first factor level, Standard, is the reference.
contrasts(rehab$treatment) <- contr.treatment(levels(rehab$treatment))
contrasts(rehab$treatment)

contr.treatment() creates the dummy-coding matrix. Assigning it with contrasts() tells R to use this coding when fitting a model with the treatment factor. Printing the matrix shows how each treatment is represented.

title: Beyond MLR Lab 1: Modeling center as a fixed effect
text:
Code center using effects coding
The sum-to-zero constraint makes each \(c_j\) a deviation from the equally weighted average across centers, comparing patients receiving the same treatment. With standard care coded 0, the intercept \(\beta_0\) is the expected standard-care outcome averaged equally across the six centers. In this balanced trial, equal weighting of centers also agrees with weighting by their patient counts.
We use effects coding to estimate these deviations directly. With dummy coding for center instead, the intercept would describe standard care in a reference center, and the other center coefficients would describe differences from that center.

contrasts(rehab$center) <- contr.sum(levels(rehab$center))
contrasts(rehab$center)

contr.sum() creates the effects-coding matrix. Inspect the result: there are six rows, one per center, but only five columns. Centers A–E each have a 1 in their own column and 0 in the others. Center F has \(-1\) in all five columns. Its contribution is therefore minus the sum of the other five contributions. Only five center coefficients are needed because the sum-to-zero constraint determines the sixth.
Changing the center coding changes the interpretation of the intercept and center coefficients. The fitted outcomes, estimated treatment difference and its standard error stay the same. Setting the coding explicitly makes the chosen parameterization reproducible.

title: Beyond MLR Lab 1: Modeling center as a fixed effect
section: Fit the model and read its output
text:
Fit the model and read its output

model_fixed <- lm(distance ~ treatment + center, data = rehab)
summary(model_fixed)

In an R model formula, the outcome is on the left of ~, and predictors are on the right. An intercept is included automatically. R uses the coding we assigned to the treatment and center factors.
In the output, (Intercept) estimates \(\beta_0\), and treatmentEnhanced estimates \(\beta_1\). The five center coefficients are named center1 to center5, corresponding to Centers A–E. For example, a positive center1 indicates a higher expected outcome in Center A than the center average, for either treatment. The model-predicted standard-care outcome in Center A is the intercept plus center1.






ImportantQuestion 3



Interpret the intercept, the treatment coefficient, and center1. How would you recover the contribution for Center F? Why would the intercept have a different interpretation if we used dummy coding for center?

title: Beyond MLR Lab 1: Modeling center as a fixed effect
text:
Treatment effect and uncertainty
In summary(model_fixed), the row treatmentEnhanced gives the estimated enhanced-minus-standard difference, its standard error, and a test against a zero difference. The residual standard error at the bottom of the output estimates the individual-error standard deviation after accounting for treatment and center.
Use confint() to obtain the 95% confidence interval for the treatment coefficient, and sigma() to extract the residual standard deviation.

confint(model_fixed, "treatmentEnhanced")
sigma(model_fixed)

The standard error of the treatment coefficient describes uncertainty about the estimated treatment difference. The residual standard deviation describes the remaining variation in individual walking distances. Both are expressed in meters.






ImportantQuestion 4



What are the estimated enhanced-minus-standard difference, its standard error, and its 95% confidence interval? What is the residual standard deviation, and how does its interpretation differ from that of the treatment coefficient’s standard error?








TipModel answer 4








Quantity
Value (m)




Enhanced minus standard
11.03


Standard error of treatment estimate
4.34


95% CI: lower limit
2.43


95% CI: upper limit
19.63


Residual standard deviation
23.76





After accounting for center, enhanced care is estimated to improve mean walking distance by 11.03 m. The 95% confidence interval is 2.43 to 19.63 m. It excludes zero, consistent with the two-sided test in the model output (\(t = 2.54\), 113 residual degrees of freedom, \(p = 0.0124\)). Under the model assumptions, the data support a positive average treatment effect. Assessing the practical importance of this improvement requires a relevant clinical benchmark.
The standard error of 4.34 m measures the sampling uncertainty in the estimated treatment difference. The residual standard deviation of 23.76 m measures the remaining variation in individual patient outcomes around their fitted treatment-and-center means.

Set the working directory
The working directory is the folder R uses as the starting point for relative file paths. For example, "data/rehabilitation_week1.csv" tells R to look inside the data subfolder of its working directory. Relative paths used to save output also start from this folder.
For this lab, set the working directory to week1, which contains your script and the data folder. Saving or opening a script does not by itself guarantee that R uses that folder as its working directory.

Run getwd() in the Console to check the selected folder. It should be week1, not its data subfolder. Check this again when starting a new session. These controls are part of RStudio’s working-directory tools.

Install pak once
An R package provides additional functions, for example for drawing figures or fitting statistical models. Throughout this course, we will use the package manager pak to install the packages we need. It also handles their dependencies: other packages they need to work.
First, install pak itself by running the following command in the Console. You only need to do this once for your current R installation; skip this step if you already have pak installed.

install.packages("pak", repos = "https://cloud.r-project.org")

title: Beyond MLR Lab 1: Modeling center as a fixed effect
text:
Use pak throughout the course
Installing a package saves it on your computer. Loading a package makes its functions available in the current R session. Installed packages remain available between sessions, but you need to load them again when you start a new session.
We will follow the same pattern in each lab: load pak with library(pak), use pkg_install() to install the packages needed for that lab, and then load those packages with library(). The pak package manager checks the required packages and their dependencies and keeps already installed versions when they meet the requirements.
For this lab, we need ggplot2 for figures and dplyr for summaries. Add the following code to the beginning of your script and run it. If pak asks whether to proceed, confirm the installation and wait for it to finish.

library(pak)
pkg_install(c("ggplot2", "dplyr"))

Now load the packages for your analysis. Keep these commands in your script so that they run each time you start the lab in a new R session.

title: Beyond MLR Lab 1: Modeling center as a fixed effect
text:
Read the data
With week1 as your working directory and the dataset saved in its data subfolder, run the following code. If R cannot find the file, check getwd(), the folder containing the CSV file, and its filename.

rehab <- read.csv("data/rehabilitation_week1.csv")

# Specify the order of the categories explicitly.
rehab$treatment <- factor(rehab$treatment,
                          levels = c("Standard", "Enhanced"))
rehab$center <- factor(rehab$center,
                       levels = paste("Center", LETTERS[1:6]))

head(rehab)
str(rehab)
table(rehab$center, rehab$treatment)

Each row represents one patient. The variables are center, treatment, and distance (six-minute walk distance in meters). A factor tells R that a variable represents categories rather than a continuous measurement. The order of the factor levels will matter when we choose how to represent these categories in the model.






ImportantQuestion 1



Check the allocation table. How many patients are in each treatment group within each center? Why is this allocation useful when comparing the treatments?

title: Beyond MLR Lab 1: Modeling center as a fixed effect
text:
Specify the model
Let \(Y_{ij}\) be the outcome for patient \(i\) in center \(j\), and let \(T_{ij}\) indicate the patient’s treatment. We include an intercept \(\beta_0\), a treatment coefficient \(\beta_1\), and a fixed contribution \(c_j\) for each center:
\[
Y_{ij} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 T_{ij} + c_j + \varepsilon_{ij},
\qquad \varepsilon_{ij} \overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim} N(0,\sigma^2).
\]
Without a constraint, increasing the intercept and decreasing every center contribution by the same amount would leave the model’s predictions unchanged. To define these parameters uniquely, we require the six center contributions to sum to zero:
\[
c_A+c_B+c_C+c_D+c_E+c_F=0.
\]
The model assumes that the expected treatment difference is the same in every center: it contains no treatment-by-center interaction. After accounting for treatment and center, the remaining errors are assumed to be independent and identically distributed Normal variables with mean zero and common variance.
To fit this model in R, we explicitly set how each factor is represented numerically. We use dummy coding for treatment to define \(T_{ij}\) and effects coding for center so that R estimates the center deviations specified above.

title: Beyond MLR Lab 1: Modeling center as a fixed effect
text:
Code treatment using dummy coding
With dummy coding, one category is the reference. We use standard care as the reference and represent treatment by a single indicator:



Treatment
Indicator \(T_{ij}\)




Standard
0


Enhanced
1



Within center \(j\), the expected standard-care outcome is \(\beta_0+c_j\), and the expected enhanced-care outcome is \(\beta_0+\beta_1+c_j\). The treatment coefficient \(\beta_1\) is therefore the enhanced-minus-standard difference.

# The first factor level, Standard, is the reference.
contrasts(rehab$treatment) <- contr.treatment(levels(rehab$treatment))
contrasts(rehab$treatment)

contr.treatment() creates the dummy-coding matrix. Assigning it with contrasts() tells R to use this coding when fitting a model with the treatment factor. Printing the matrix shows how each treatment is represented.

title: Beyond MLR Lab 1: Modeling center as a fixed effect
text:
Code center using effects coding
The sum-to-zero constraint makes each \(c_j\) a deviation from the equally weighted average across centers, comparing patients receiving the same treatment. With standard care coded 0, the intercept \(\beta_0\) is the expected standard-care outcome averaged equally across the six centers. It does not average over the two treatments. In this balanced trial, equal weighting of centers also agrees with weighting by their patient counts.
We use effects coding to estimate these deviations directly. With dummy coding for center instead, the intercept would describe standard care in a reference center, and the other center coefficients would describe differences from that center.

contrasts(rehab$center) <- contr.sum(levels(rehab$center))
contrasts(rehab$center)

contr.sum() creates the effects-coding matrix. Inspect the result: there are six rows, one per center, but only five columns. Centers A–E each have a 1 in their own column and 0 in the others. Center F has \(-1\) in all five columns. Its contribution is therefore minus the sum of the other five contributions; it is not set to zero. Only five center coefficients are needed because the sum-to-zero constraint determines the sixth.
Changing the center coding changes the interpretation of the intercept and center coefficients, but does not change the fitted outcomes or the estimated treatment difference and its standard error. Setting the coding explicitly ensures that the analysis does not depend on previously changed global R options.

title: Beyond MLR Lab 1: Modeling center as a fixed effect
section: Fit the model and read its output
text:
Fit the model and read its output

model_fixed <- lm(distance ~ treatment + center, data = rehab)
summary(model_fixed)

In an R model formula, the outcome is on the left of ~, and predictors are on the right. An intercept is included automatically. R uses the coding we assigned to the treatment and center factors.
In the output, (Intercept) estimates \(\beta_0\), and treatmentEnhanced estimates \(\beta_1\). The five center coefficients are named center1 to center5, corresponding to Centers A–E. For example, a positive center1 indicates a higher expected outcome in Center A than the center average, for either treatment. The model-predicted standard-care outcome in Center A is the intercept plus center1.






ImportantQuestion 3



Interpret the intercept, the treatment coefficient, and center1. How would you recover the contribution for Center F? Why would the intercept have a different interpretation if we used dummy coding for center?

title: Beyond MLR Lab 1: Modeling center as a fixed effect
text:
Treatment effect and uncertainty
In summary(model_fixed), the row treatmentEnhanced gives the estimated enhanced-minus-standard difference, its standard error, and a test against a zero difference. The residual standard error at the bottom of the output estimates the individual-error standard deviation after accounting for treatment and center.
Use confint() to obtain the 95% confidence interval for the treatment coefficient, and sigma() to extract the residual standard deviation.

confint(model_fixed, "treatmentEnhanced")
sigma(model_fixed)

The standard error of the treatment coefficient describes uncertainty about the estimated treatment difference. The residual standard deviation describes the remaining variation in individual walking distances. Both are expressed in meters.






ImportantQuestion 4



What are the estimated enhanced-minus-standard difference, its standard error, and its 95% confidence interval? What is the residual standard deviation, and how does its interpretation differ from that of the treatment coefficient’s standard error?

title: Beyond MLR Lab 2: Modeling center as a random effect
text:
In Lab 1, we analyzed a simulated rehabilitation trial involving 120 patients after knee replacement in six centers. Each center assigned 10 patients to standard care and 10 to enhanced rehabilitation. We fitted a model containing separate fixed center effects.
We now keep the same randomized block design and the same question: What is the difference in expected six-minute walk distance at 12 weeks between enhanced and standard care, and how precisely is it estimated? Instead of estimating separate fixed center parameters, we describe center contributions using a distribution. This also allows us to quantify variation between centers.
By the end of this lab, you should be able to fit a random-intercept model, interpret its treatment estimate and uncertainty, interpret its variance components and intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC), and assess its conditional residuals.

title: Beyond MLR Lab 2: Modeling center as a random effect
text:
Extract the variances
VarCorr() returns the estimated variance components. Converting its output to a data frame makes it straightforward to use the values in a calculation.

variance_components <- as.data.frame(VarCorr(model_random))
variance_components

center_variance <- variance_components$vcov[
  variance_components$grp == "center"
]
patient_variance <- variance_components$vcov[
  variance_components$grp == "Residual"
]

c(center_variance = center_variance,
  patient_variance = patient_variance)

The vcov column contains variances; the sdcor column contains their standard deviations for this model. Use the variances, not the standard deviations, in the intraclass correlation coefficient calculation.

title: Beyond MLR Lab 2: Modeling center as a random effect
text:
Introduce the intraclass correlation
After accounting for treatment, the remaining outcome variation consists of the shared center contribution and the individual error:
\[
u_{ij}=c_j+\varepsilon_{ij},
\qquad \operatorname{Var}(u_{ij})=\sigma_c^2+\sigma^2.
\]
For two different patients in the same center, the shared center contribution gives
\[
\operatorname{Cov}(u_{ij},u_{kj})=\sigma_c^2 \quad (i\ne k).
\]
Dividing this covariance by the common variance gives the intraclass correlation coefficient:
\[
\mathrm{ICC}=\frac{\sigma_c^2}{\sigma_c^2+\sigma^2}.
\]
This has two connected interpretations:

The proportion of outcome variance remaining after accounting for treatment that is attributable to differences between centers.
The correlation between outcomes of two different patients in the same center, after accounting for their treatments and averaging over the modeled center distribution.

If we condition on a particular center effect as well as treatment, only the independent individual errors remain. The within-center correlation above arises because patients share a random center contribution.

icc <- center_variance / (center_variance + patient_variance)
icc







ImportantQuestion 4



Calculate the intraclass correlation coefficient. Interpret it both as a variance proportion and as a within-center correlation. What correlation does the model assume for patients in different centers, after accounting for treatment?

title: Beyond MLR Lab 3: Treatment effects across laboratories
text:
Five laboratories compare a standard treatment with an experimental treatment in a simulated wound-healing experiment. Each laboratory uses 20 independent cell-culture plates and randomly assigns 10 plates to each treatment. Each plate is measured once, 48 hours after treatment. The outcome is the percentage of the original wound area that has closed. Higher values indicate more closure.
This is a randomized block design, with laboratory as the blocking factor. The experimental unit is the cell-culture plate. The dataset contains 100 observations simulated for teaching.
Our question is: How do the estimated treatment effects vary across laboratories, and how much improvement is estimated within each laboratory? We treat the five laboratories as fixed and focus on treatment comparisons within these laboratories.
By the end of this lab, you should be able to explore an interaction, fit and interpret a fixed interaction model, estimate simple treatment effects, and assess the model assumptions.






NoteWorking through the lab



Run the code in order in an R script, and record your answers to the questions. The lab page shows the code; you generate the results yourself.

title: Beyond MLR Lab 3: Treatment effects across laboratories
text:
Specify the model and coding
Use the same model structure as in the lecture, replacing center with laboratory. Let \(Y_{ij}\) be the wound closure for plate \(i\) in laboratory \(j\), and let \(T_{ij}=0\) for standard treatment and \(T_{ij}=1\) for experimental treatment:
\[
Y_{ij} = \beta_0 + c_j + (\beta_1+d_j)T_{ij} + \varepsilon_{ij}.
\]
With effects coding for laboratory, the deviations satisfy
\[
\sum_{j=1}^{5} c_j = 0, \qquad \sum_{j=1}^{5} d_j = 0.
\]

\(\beta_0\) is the standard-treatment mean averaged equally across laboratories.
\(c_j\) is laboratory \(j\)’s deviation from that standard-treatment average.
\(\beta_1\) is the treatment effect averaged equally across laboratories.
\(d_j\) is laboratory \(j\)’s deviation from that average treatment effect.
\(\varepsilon_{ij}\) is the plate’s individual error. The model assumes independent Normal errors with mean zero and a common variance.

Thus, the treatment effect in laboratory \(j\) is \(\beta_1+d_j\). Set dummy coding for treatment and effects coding for laboratory explicitly, as in Week 1.

contrasts(wound$treatment) <- contr.treatment(levels(wound$treatment))
contrasts(wound$laboratory) <- contr.sum(levels(wound$laboratory))

contrasts(wound$treatment)
contrasts(wound$laboratory)

title: Beyond MLR Lab 3: Treatment effects across laboratories
text:
Fit the interaction model

model_full <- lm(closure ~ treatment * laboratory, data = wound)
summary(model_full)
confint(model_full)

The * includes treatment, laboratory, and their interaction. It is shorthand for treatment + laboratory + treatment:laboratory.
In the coefficient table, (Intercept) estimates \(\beta_0\) and treatmentExperimental estimates \(\beta_1\). The rows laboratory1 to laboratory4 estimate the baseline deviations for Laboratories A to D. The rows treatmentExperimental:laboratory1 to treatmentExperimental:laboratory4 estimate their treatment-effect deviations. Laboratory E’s deviations are minus the sums of the corresponding four coefficients.
The interaction coefficient for a laboratory is its deviation from the average treatment effect. Its p-value tests whether that deviation is zero. The simple treatment effect in that laboratory combines this deviation with the treatment coefficient.






ImportantQuestion 3



Interpret the intercept and the treatment coefficient. Use the coefficients to calculate the estimated experimental-minus-standard treatment effect in Laboratory A. How would you calculate the corresponding effect in Laboratory E?

title: Beyond MLR Lab 3: Treatment effects across laboratories
text:
Obtain estimated marginal means
Estimated marginal means (EMMs) are model-based estimates of group means, averaged over other factors where appropriate. We obtain these means from the fitted interaction model, then compare them to estimate treatment effects.
For simple treatment effects, keep laboratories separate and estimate the standard and experimental mean within each laboratory.

treatment_means <- emmeans(model_full, ~ treatment | laboratory)
treatment_means

Here, model_full supplies the fitted model and ~ treatment | laboratory requests treatment means separately within each laboratory. The command calculates these means from the fitted model.
In the output, emmean is the estimated mean closure, SE is its estimated standard error, and lower.CL and upper.CL are its 95% confidence limits. The interaction model fits a separate mean for every treatment-laboratory combination, so these estimated means equal the observed cell means in the exploratory summary.

title: Beyond MLR Lab 3: Treatment effects across laboratories
text:
Compare treatments within laboratories
Use pairs() to compare the two predicted means within each laboratory, then summary() to display the treatment differences with pointwise 95% confidence intervals and unadjusted p-values.

simple_effects <- pairs(treatment_means, reverse = TRUE, adjust = "none")
summary(simple_effects, infer = c(TRUE, TRUE), by = NULL)

Because the treatment levels are ordered Standard then Experimental, reverse = TRUE gives experimental minus standard. The column estimate contains the simple treatment effect in each laboratory, measured in percentage points.
In pairs(), adjust = "none" specifies pointwise intervals and unadjusted p-values. The summary() call uses this setting: infer = c(TRUE, TRUE) requests both confidence intervals and tests, and by = NULL displays the five comparisons together. Each p-value tests whether the treatment effect in that laboratory is zero.
The standard error for a difference describes uncertainty about that treatment effect. It accounts for the covariance between the predicted means. Use this standard error when interpreting the treatment comparison.






ImportantQuestion 4



Interpret the estimated treatment effect and its 95% confidence interval in Laboratory A. Check that its estimate agrees with your calculation from the regression coefficients. What do the estimates, confidence intervals, and unadjusted p-values suggest about the treatment effect within each laboratory? Describe the size and uncertainty of the estimated effects.








NoteOptional: considering multiple comparisons





When several treatment comparisons are interpreted together, an adjustment can help control the probability of at least one false-positive finding across the set. Whether this is appropriate depends on the scientific questions and how the comparisons will be used.
The Bonferroni correction multiplies each p-value by the number of comparisons, with a maximum of 1. Compare the adjusted p-values with 0.05. For example, across five comparisons, a p-value of 0.008 becomes 0.040.
To apply the correction, change adjust = "none" to adjust = "bonferroni" in the pairs() call above and rerun it, followed by the same summary() call. With by = NULL, the correction applies across all five laboratory comparisons. This also adjusts the confidence intervals.

title: Week 1 assignment: Comparing protein extraction protocols
text:
Study description
A laboratory wants to compare a standard protein extraction protocol with a modified protocol. The aim is to determine whether the modified protocol increases protein yield while accounting for differences between tissue donors.
Tissue from each of ten donors is divided into eight aliquots. Within each donor, four aliquots are randomly assigned to the standard protocol and four to the modified protocol. Each aliquot undergoes its assigned extraction protocol and is measured once, giving 80 observations.
The outcome is protein yield, measured in micrograms of extracted protein per milligram of tissue (µg/mg). Larger values indicate a higher yield. These are simulated teaching data.


Dataset
Each row represents one tissue aliquot.



Variable
Description




aliquot
Unique identifier for the aliquot


donor
Tissue donor, labelled Donor 01 to Donor 10


protocol
Extraction protocol: Standard or Modified


protein_yield
Protein yield in µg/mg





Analysis tasks

Describe the design. Identify the experimental unit and blocking variable, and explain how the protocols were assigned within donors.
Explore the data. Create a plot showing individual protein yields, protocol-specific means within each donor, and overall protocol means. Discuss whether the plot suggests substantial differences between donors, considering both the donor-specific means and the variation among aliquots within donors.
Fit a random-intercept model. Include protocol as a fixed effect and a random intercept for donor. Use dummy coding for protocol, with Standard as the reference. Interpret the intercept and protocol coefficient. Explain what the random donor intercept represents and what the model assumes about the protocol difference across donors.
Interpret the results. Obtain the modified-minus-standard difference, its estimated standard error and its 95% confidence interval. Report and interpret the estimated donor and residual variances. Calculate and interpret the intraclass correlation coefficient.
Check the model and conclude. Examine conditional-residual diagnostic plots and comment on the model assumptions. Write a short conclusion answering the laboratory’s question, including the estimated protocol difference, its uncertainty and appropriate units.

Use the Week 1 labs as references when constructing your analysis. Explain your findings in the context of protein extraction and include units where appropriate.


Report and submission
For this assignment, submit a report created using Quarto that presents your analysis, results and interpretations, using the template provided in the Downloads section below.
The template starts with a setup chunk that uses pak to install the required analysis packages if needed and then loads them. Install pak itself as described in Lab 1 if you have not already done so. The setup chunk runs when you render the document, but its code and output are hidden from the report. The template’s opening instructions follow the folder structure introduced in Lab 1. Expand Help with Quarto below for instructions on running code and rendering your report.
Submit both the completed Quarto source file (.qmd) and the rendered HTML report. Keep your analysis code, results and figures visible in the report, and accompany them with your interpretations. Only the setup chunk is hidden.






NoteHelp with Quarto





This assignment combines independent data analysis with practice in documenting and communicating your results. Use the supplied Quarto template as a starting point; you may adjust its structure to suit your report.
What a Quarto file contains
A Quarto file is a plain text file with the .qmd extension. It contains three main elements:

A YAML header enclosed by three dashes (---), which defines metadata and global options.
R code chunks enclosed by three backticks, with {r} immediately after the opening backticks. These contain executable R code.
Narrative text written in Markdown, including your explanations and interpretations.

Organize and render your report
Follow the folder structure introduced in Lab 1: save the template in your week1 folder and the dataset in week1/data. Read the dataset using read.csv("data/protein_yield.csv").
Open the .qmd file in RStudio. To try code as you work, use the Run button in a code chunk or select lines and press Ctrl+Enter on Windows/Linux or Cmd+Enter on macOS. To produce the complete HTML report, save the file and press Render. Alternatively, with week1 as the current directory in the RStudio Terminal, run:
quarto render report_template.qmd
If you renamed the template, use your chosen filename in this command. Rendering executes the R code using knitr to produce an intermediate Markdown (.md) file containing the code and its output. Pandoc then processes this file to generate the final HTML report. Include the data import and all analysis steps in the document so the report can be reproduced by rendering it.
Global execution settings
Global execution settings are defined under execute in the YAML header. For example:
---
title: "Analysis report"
author: "Your name"
format:
  html:
    toc: true
    toc-depth: 2
    embed-resources: true
execute:
  eval: true
  echo: true
  warning: false
  message: false
---
These options determine how code chunks are handled throughout the document:

eval: true executes the chunks by default.
echo: true includes the analysis code in the rendered report.
warning: false and message: false suppress warnings and messages in the rendered output.

The supplied template already contains suitable settings, so you can use its existing YAML header as your starting point. It leaves warnings visible while you develop the analysis. Keep eval: true and echo: true for this assignment so your analysis runs and its code and results are included.
Options for individual chunks
You can override global settings for an individual chunk by adding lines beginning with #|, followed by option: value, at the top of the chunk. For example:
```{r}
#| eval: false
summary(my_data)
```
Here, eval: false overrides the global setting, so this chunk is displayed but not executed. Other commonly used options include include: false, which hides both the code and its output while allowing the chunk to run when eval: true, and echo: false, which hides the code while retaining its output.
For this assignment, keep your analysis code, results and figures visible. The supplied setup chunk is the exception: it uses include: false to install and load packages without displaying its code or output.
Further reading
The following chapters of R for Data Science (2nd edition) provide more detail:

Quarto formats: Chapter 29 describes the available output formats.
